newsitem.title: USA: Oklahoma City seeks answers, healing from trial.
newsitem.headline: Oklahoma City seeks answers, healing from trial.

text.p: Still haunted by the worst bombing ever on U.S. soil, survivors of the Oklahoma City blast hope the trial of chief suspect Timothy McVeigh will bring the worst of their torment to a close.

Virtually everyone in this city believes McVeigh is guilty, and his relaxed manner in pre-trial hearings has infuriated relatives and friends of the 168 people killed in the massive explosion on April 19, 1995.
With jury selection set to open in Denver on March 31, the victims say they want a fast, clean trial with a guilty verdict and a death penalty.

"We just hope the evidence will prove he is guilty beyond any possible doubt so there can be no retrial. We don't want a mistrial," said Patti Hall, whose legs were crushed in the blast, requiring extensive surgery and other treatment.
Others said they need more than just a conviction.

"I want to know why. Why did he do it? What were his goals? What did he plan to achieve? What was his theory? What was his great plan?," asked Tina Tomlin, whose husband Rick died in the blast. "I just want to know the truth, all of it."

Prosecutors allege McVeigh, a Gulf War veteran, and his Army buddy Terry Nichols became fanatics of the right-wing militia movement and blew up the Alfred P. Murrah federal building as part of a plan to topple the government.

Both men have pleaded not guilty and Nichols' lawyers were successful in pushing for separate trials. The evidence against McVeigh appears to be stronger and, in Oklahoma City, he is the target of the survivors' hatred. Many hope they will find it easier to cope with their losses if and when McVeigh is convicted and sentenced to death.

"Until this trial is over I don't feel I can get on with my life. I'm living in a vacuum right now. You can't plan anything down the road with all this hanging over you," said Roy Sells, who lost his wife of 17 years, Lee Sells.

That sense of desperation has been heightened by long delays in bringing the case to trial and the decision to move it from Oklahoma to Denver, which left many family members feeling betrayed by the justice system.

For most of those who have lost loved ones, the last two years have brought a series of emotional crises. Some have crumbled emotionally or isolated themselves and others have banded together by setting up and attending support groups.

Marsha Kight, whose daughter Frankie Merrill was killed, set up Families and Survivors United, which meets regularly, has its own Internet site and plans to publish a book in memory of the victims. She also has taken on a high-profile role in calling for constitutional reform to better protect the victims of violent crime.
"If there is anything positive at all we can do from something as horrific as this, it is to make changes," Kight said. "I don't want all those lives to be in vain."
